filled_passage:
For our exhibition, we built a marble run from cardboard tubes. A marble was to travel down a stand into a cup. The first few tubes seemed fine. After we added the last section, however, the marble stopped halfway.

Leo wanted a faster marble; I wanted a larger cup. Our teacher asked us to watch where the marble actually stopped. It had not reached the cup, so a different cup could not solve the problem.

We tried again and marked the stopping point. The final tube sloped upwards: its far end was higher than its entrance. Our paper mountains had hidden it.

We removed part of the painted mountain to adjust the track. I was disappointed to take apart my work, but lowering that end let the marble reach the cup. I began replacing the paper. Leo asked me to wait: he wanted another test first.

We tested five times. On the fourth, a loose join moved and the marble fell out. We taped it firmly and repeated the tests before replacing the mountain.

At the exhibition, a pupil asked about a square flap in the paper. I lifted it to show the tubes. What had first looked like damage was now a useful window into the model.

Some pupils wanted to race two marbles. We explained that our track was built for one at a time. We did not claim it could do more than we had tested.

We kept a photograph and a list of changes. One showed how the model looked; the other explained how it worked. I still valued the painted mountain, but also the work beneath it, usually hidden from view.

Leo and I were solving one problem together, rather than defending separate ideas. Before packing up, we checked for the final marble. Nothing was missing—except our first guess about needing a faster marble. We were happy to leave that one behind.
